Troops, Prosecutions, and a Shutdown Weaponized

A week when courts blocked military deployments over and over, prosecutors were purged for refusing to charge the president's rivals, and the shutdown became a tool of political retaliation

```markdown This was the week the machinery of federal power collided, repeatedly, with the limits meant to restrain it. Over seven days, a president tried to put troops in American cities over the objections of their governors, the Justice Department indicted two of his most prominent adversaries after career prosecutors said the evidence didn't support charges, and a government shutdown entering its second week hardened into a tool of political pressure. Courts pushed back at nearly every turn. The administration, just as often, tried to work around them.

**The Weekend**

The weekend opened with dueling deployments. Trump ordered federalized Illinois National Guard troops into Chicago and, separately, sent Guard forces into Portland, in each case over the objections of state officials — Governor JB Pritzker in Illinois, state leaders in Oregon. In Oregon, Judge Karin Immergut, a Trump appointee, moved fast: she issued a restraining order on Saturday blocking the deployment, calling the administration's justification "untethered to the facts." The government's response came within hours, not days — officials tried to reroute California and Texas Guard troops into Portland instead. Immergut broadened her order on Sunday to bar deployment from any state, a sign of what would become the week's defining rhythm: an executive branch testing the edges of a judicial order almost as soon as it was issued.

On the ground, federal agents met protesters outside ICE facilities in Portland and in Broadview, Illinois, with tear gas, pepper spray, and pepper balls. One target was a demonstrator in an inflatable frog costume, an image that quickly became a viral emblem of the protests and spawned a mocking counter-movement dubbed "Operation Inflation." Journalists and legal observers covering the Broadview demonstrations were also hit with tear gas and physical force. In a separate and more serious incident, Border Patrol agents shot 30-year-old Marimar Martinez during a vehicle pursuit in Chicago's Brighton Park neighborhood; DHS said agents fired after being rammed, but her attorney disputed that account, citing body-camera footage, and a judge ordered her released pending trial. The facts of the shooting remained contested even as the week moved on.

Rhetoric matched the physical confrontations. Trump's account posted an AI-generated video depicting Democrats as zombies hunted by a Grim Reaper, along with images branding the party "the party of hate, evil, and Satan." Stephen Miller, the president's deputy chief of staff, called Immergut's ruling "legal insurrection" and described protest opposition as "leftwing terrorism" shielded by "far-left" judges and prosecutors — the first installment of language that would escalate as the week went on. Reporting also surfaced showing how much authority had concentrated in Miller himself, who was said to be directing deportation and detention policy while exercising more influence over military strikes on Venezuelan drug boats than Secretary of State Rubio. Elsewhere, smaller but telling stories accumulated: a plan to mint a coin bearing Trump's image despite a law barring living presidents from currency, Trump's own admission that the shutdown was designed to make the Affordable Care Act unaffordable, and Speaker Mike Johnson's decision to delay the House's return — and with it the swearing-in of newly elected Rep. Adelita Grijalva, whose vote would complete a discharge petition on the Epstein files.

**Monday**

The confrontation widened into new terrain. CNN reported on a classified Justice Department legal opinion arguing the president could unilaterally designate drug traffickers as "enemy combatants" subject to killing without congressional authorization or judicial review — a claim of war power far beyond anything Congress had granted. The same day, Trump approved a 211-mile mining road through Alaskan wilderness previously blocked on environmental grounds, while the administration purchased a 10% equity stake in Trilogy Metals, a move that lifted major donor John Paulson's stake from roughly $30 million to more than $100 million.

But the week's defining story began to take shape Monday as well. Career prosecutor Elizabeth Yusi had found insufficient probable cause to charge New York Attorney General Letitia James with mortgage fraud. Her colleagues Maya Song and Michael Ben'Ary were fired amid pressure to bring cases against both James and former FBI Director James Comey. A grand jury under Lindsey Halligan, a Trump-appointed prosecutor, had already indicted Comey days earlier. In response, a coalition of 282 former Justice Department officials issued a letter warning that the department was being turned into a political weapon. Separately, FBI Director Kash Patel fired several agents who had been photographed kneeling during a 2020 protest, in what a White House official privately described as an effort to please the president. And the disinformation continued: the Oregon Republican Party circulated a fabricated composite image purporting to show Portland unrest, while Miller falsely claimed nightly "street battles" with antifa in Portland — remarks made the same day a federal judge's home was targeted by arson.

**Tuesday**

The shutdown took a turn toward overt coercion. The White House budget office reversed prior guidance to argue that furloughed federal workers were not automatically entitled to statutory back pay, while Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt warned of coming layoffs and cuts to food assistance for low-income mothers and children. The Senate rejected competing funding bills for a fifth time. In Chicago, Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul sued to block federalization of the state's Guard and the deployment of out-of-state troops; Judge April Perry declined to immediately halt Texas Guard forces already en route, setting a midnight deadline for the government to respond. Attorney General Pam Bondi appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee and largely declined to answer substantive questions about the prosecutions, the deployments, or the Epstein files, instead making personal attacks on senators and citing the shutdown as a distraction. Comey's legal team signaled it would argue his prosecution was vindictive and selective, and would separately challenge the legitimacy of Halligan's appointment. Six former surgeons general, appointed under presidents of both parties, published a joint warning that Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s leadership at Health and Human Services was endangering public trust and national health.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday escalated further. Trump posted that Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson and Governor Pritzker should be jailed for "failing to protect" ICE officers; Pritzker answered by calling Trump a "wannabe dictator" and daring him, "come and get me." The exchange came as Texas National Guard troops began arriving near Chicago even as Illinois's lawsuit proceeded. NBC News reported that administration officials were engaged in increasingly serious internal discussions about invoking the Insurrection Act — a statute not used against a state's wishes since the civil rights era — though no imminent decision was expected; Trump himself said he would consider it if "people were being killed" or if governors and courts "held us up." Comey was arraigned and pleaded not guilty to charges of lying to Congress, with his lawyers previewing motions to dismiss on both vindictive-prosecution and improper-appointment grounds; the presiding judge voiced early skepticism that the case was as complicated as prosecutors claimed. Bondi again stonewalled the Senate, including on whether the FBI had found photographs of Trump with Jeffrey Epstein, even as reporting revealed that DHS and the FBI had reassigned hundreds of national security specialists and roughly a quarter of all FBI agents nationwide to immigration enforcement. In Texas, Attorney General Ken Paxton opened investigations into what he called "radical leftist organizations," part of a broader post-Kirk-assassination effort to tie the "radical left" to political violence.

**Thursday**

Thursday was the week's heaviest single day. A grand jury under Halligan indicted Letitia James on bank fraud and false statement charges tied to a 2020 mortgage — the same case career prosecutor Elizabeth Yusi had found lacked probable cause. Halligan herself presented the case to the grand jury, an unusual step for a U.S. Attorney. James called the charges political retaliation for her earlier fraud case against Trump. Hours later, Judge April Perry issued a two-week restraining order blocking the federalized deployment to Illinois outright, finding "no credible evidence" of the rebellion the administration had cited; Judge Sara Ellis separately barred federal agents from using force against journalists and protesters without probable cause and ordered agents to visibly identify themselves. In the Senate, a vote of 48–51 effectively ceded congressional oversight of lethal force against drug cartels, ratifying authority already used in Caribbean strikes that had killed at least 21 people without evidence shared with Congress. Trump also announced 100% tariffs on Chinese goods effective November 1, canceled a planned meeting with President Xi, and rattled financial markets. He issued a Columbus Day proclamation describing modern historical scholarship as "left-wing arson," held an "Antifa Roundtable" with figures including Jack Posobiec at which Bondi and Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem compared the loosely organized movement to a terrorist group, and the Pentagon introduced new press restrictions that CNN said it would not sign. The administration also confirmed it had withdrawn from all pending Section 2 Voting Rights Act cases, and a Rutgers historian who had written on anti-fascism and received death threats, Mark Bray, was briefly blocked from boarding an international flight the day after Trump vowed action against antifa.

**Friday**

The week closed without resolution. OMB Director Russell Vought carried out layoffs of more than 4,000 federal workers, and shutdown-driven cuts eliminated the CDC's entire ethics office, its institutional review board, its library, and its Washington policy liaison office — roughly 1,300 positions in all, some involving employees a court had already ruled protected. Federal unions filed an emergency motion to block the layoffs as unlawful. Reporting confirmed that Erik Siebert, the U.S. Attorney who had declined to prosecute Comey and James, had been removed for that refusal, closing the loop on the week's prosecutorial purge; separately, Federal Housing Finance Agency Director William Pulte made criminal referrals against Trump critics including James, Adam Schiff, and Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, bypassing standard ethics procedures. In Chicago, WGN-TV producer Debbie Brockman was arrested by masked Border Patrol agents while filming a detention — one day after Judge Ellis's order specifically protecting journalists from such treatment — and held roughly seven hours before release without charges. Speaker Johnson and Whip Tom Emmer branded the planned October 18 "No Kings" protest a "hate America rally" led by "the terrorist wing" of the Democratic Party, while Johnson canceled a fourth consecutive week of House session, further delaying Grijalva's swearing-in; senators Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth were separately denied access to an ICE facility for oversight visits. The USDA warned that food assistance for 42 million Americans could lapse November 1, confirming it would not tap a $5 billion emergency reserve to prevent it. Amid all this, Oklahoma Governor Kevin Stitt, chair of the National Governors Association, became the first Republican governor to publicly criticize the deployments, warning the precedent could one day be turned against Republican-led states.

Taken as a whole, the week showed two systems working in direct tension. Courts — including judges appointed by Trump himself — repeatedly found that the government's stated justifications for military deployment and use of force did not hold up, and they said so in writing, with specific findings rather than vague gestures. At the same time, enforcement on the ground, personnel decisions inside the Justice Department, and rhetoric from the White House moved in the opposite direction, treating judicial rulings as obstacles to route around rather than binding constraints. A prosecutor's finding of no probable cause was overridden by removing the prosecutor. A restraining order protecting journalists was followed, within a day, by the arrest of a journalist. A shutdown born of ordinary budget disagreement became, by the administration's own admission, a lever against a rival party's programs and constituents. Whether the courts' repeated interventions ultimately hold, or whether they are absorbed and bypassed as this week's pattern suggests, is likely to shape how much practical meaning judicial checks retain in the months ahead. ```
